title: A life of practice, closed
hook: a whole life of practice in three short lines
tomorrow: one full moon holds three of the Buddha's biggest days. which three?

segments.voice: Yesterday, saying the vow: Angulimala's sentence, fixed until it was true, then said aloud. Said aloud. Today the block closes, on three short lines.

At every retirement party, someone raises a glass and tries to sum up a whole career in one toast, and the toast runs long. A Chinese poet tried it in one question. Chan Buddhist tradition tells of Bai Juyi visiting a monk called Bird's Nest, who meditated in the branches of a tree. The poet asked: what is the whole of the Buddha's teaching? The monk gave him three lines. Don't do harm. Do good. Purify your mind. The poet wasn't impressed. A child of three knows that, he said. And Bird's Nest answered: a child of three may know it, but an old man of eighty still finds it hard to do.
screen: `A WHOLE CAREER IN ONE TOAST?` → `A MONK IN A TREE.` → `A CHILD KNOWS IT. AN OLD MAN CAN'T DO IT.`

segments.voice: Those three lines weren't the monk's own idea. They're verse 183 of the Dhammapada, and in Max Müller's translation they read: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Notice the end. Not one teacher's tip: the teaching of all the awakened ones. So the question has a Buddhist answer, and it fits on a sticky note. Here's the teaching inside it. Buddhists speak of the path as a training in three parts, conduct, meditation and wisdom, and one reading lays the verse over them: not harming and doing good are conduct, and purifying the mind is the work of meditation and wisdom. And Bird's Nest adds the harder part. The verse isn't hard to learn. It's hard to live, every day, for a whole life. That's why this block has been daily, weekly and yearly practice, refuge, few wants, a vow: not more to know, just more days of doing. A neighbor tradition answers the same question in three lines too. The prophet Micah, in the Hebrew Bible that Jews and Christians both read, asks in the King James Version: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Shared: a whole life, boiled down to three things you do, not three things you know. The honest difference sits in the third line. Micah's ends walking with God. The Dhammapada's ends inside your own mind, as work the verse hands to you. Neither one is the other in disguise.
screen: `DHAMMAPADA 183: THREE LINES.` · `CONDUCT, MEDITATION, WISDOM.` · `EASY TO KNOW, HARD TO LIVE.` · `MICAH: JUSTLY, MERCY, HUMBLY.` · then, large: `A LIFE OF PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Take out the vow you wrote two days ago and set it beside the three lines: don't harm, do good, purify the mind. Read your vow slowly, once, and notice which line it lives under. Then let the page rest in front of you and sit with it in the quiet.
A life of practice: in Pali, bhavana, cultivation. Three short lines, easy enough for a child to say, long enough for a whole life to do.
Here's the line: a life of practice, known by a child, still being done at eighty. Forty-five of forty-five; the block is closed.

howItsDone: In some Buddhist communities Dhammapada 183 is recited as a summary of the teaching; in practice it is lived as the threefold training of conduct, meditation and wisdom, kept up through daily, weekly and yearly practice.

chat.meaning: Dhammapada 183 gives the teaching of the awakened in three lines; Bird's Nest said a child knows them, but living them takes a lifetime.

Chan.meaning: Chinese meditation Buddhism, the root of Japanese Zen

Bai Juyi.meaning: a Chinese poet who asked for the whole teaching

Bird's Nest.meaning: a Chan monk who, tradition says, meditated in a tree

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

Micah.meaning: a prophet in the Hebrew Bible

bhavana.meaning: cultivation: practice that grows something over time

notes: Confirm Max Müller's 1881 wording of Dhammapada 183 word for word, including '(all)'.

Bird's Nest (Niaoke Daolin) and Bai Juyi: paraphrased from the Chan record (Jingde Chuandeng Lu); the 'child of three' and 'old man of eighty' figures come from that story. Confirm the source and the numbers.
'The path as a training' (sikkha: conduct, meditation, wisdom) mapped onto the verse's three lines is a common teaching reading; confirm the framing is fair.
Trapdoor: 'tradition counts it among the verses of the Ovada Patimokkha'; confirm.
Unity thread: Micah 6:8 (KJV) as the neighbor's three-line answer; difference named in the third line, no ranking. Confirm the Buddhist side ('work the verse hands to you') is fair.
Shape: wisdom (one question, the tradition's answer, a neighbor's answer). Mai's arc: Ông living with the family; Ava asks what Buddhism is.
Surprising fact: a poet called the whole teaching child's play, and a monk in a tree said an old man still can't do it.
